levels.title: Universal prevention
levels.description: Addressed to a whole population (e.g. all pupils in a class or school) regardless of their level of risk. It aims to strengthen protective factors and delay initiation before problems appear.
examples: normative education correcting beliefs about how common substance use is
work on school climate and bonds with adults
parenting-skills workshops open to all parents

levels.title: Selective prevention
levels.description: Addressed to groups at increased risk because of their life situation or environment (e.g. children from families with alcohol problems, young people in care), even though individuals do not yet show problems.
examples: socio-therapeutic groups in a day-care centre for children from families with alcohol problems
family-strengthening programme for families in crisis
mentoring for young people in a youth educational centre
alternative activities (sport, volunteering) in a high-risk neighbourhood

levels.title: Indicated prevention
levels.description: Addressed to individuals who already show early signs of problems (e.g. experimenting with substances, truancy, risky behaviour) but do not meet criteria for addiction. It aims to stop the problem from developing.
examples: brief motivational intervention after an incident at school
early-intervention programme for young people using cannabis
individual educational work with the pupil and parents
support group for young people after first contact with the family court

riskFactors.text: early and persistent problem behaviour (aggression, impulsivity)
strong need for stimulation and sensation seeking
emotional difficulties and lack of ways to cope with stress
substance use by parents or siblings and permissive attitudes at home
poor parental monitoring and unclear rules
academic failure, especially from the early grades
low bonding with school and low commitment to learning
easy availability of alcohol, tobacco and drugs
community norms favourable to substance use
poverty, neighbourhood disorganisation and lack of leisure opportunities

protectiveFactors.text: ability to regulate emotions and control impulses
plans and goals for the future
beliefs and values that do not favour substance use
strong, warm bond with at least one parent or carer
clear rules and consistent, caring supervision
bonding with school and with at least one teacher
experiencing success and recognition at school
safe, supportive school climate with clear norms
sense of belonging to a group without pressure to use
access to after-school activities, sport and volunteering
available, trusted adults outside the family (mentors, coaches, educators)

strategies.title: Normative education
strategies.description: Correcting overestimated beliefs about how many peers use substances, using reliable local or national survey data.

strategies.title: Life-skills development
strategies.description: Interactive training of personal and social skills: decision-making, coping with stress, communication, assertiveness and refusal.

strategies.title: Parent and family programmes
strategies.description: Regular sessions strengthening parenting skills, monitoring, communication and family bonds, often with children taking part.

strategies.title: Classroom management and school climate
strategies.description: Whole-school and teacher-level action building clear norms, mutual respect and a sense of belonging (e.g. programmes such as the Good Behaviour Game).

strategies.title: Environmental strategies
strategies.description: Changing the environment: enforcing bans on sales to minors, limiting availability, school substance policies, local regulations.

strategies.title: Mentoring
strategies.description: Regular, long-term meetings of a young person with a trained adult mentor who offers support and a role model.

strategies.title: Brief intervention
strategies.description: A short, structured conversation (often in the spirit of motivational interviewing) with a person showing risky behaviour.

strategies.title: Peer-led programmes
strategies.description: Sessions run by trained peer leaders under adult supervision; effectiveness depends on the quality of training and structure.

strategies.title: Alternatives
strategies.description: Offering attractive activities (sport, arts, volunteering); works mainly when combined with skills development and relationships with adults.

strategies.title: Information only
strategies.description: Lectures and leaflets about the harms of substances without work on skills and norms; may increase knowledge but do not change behaviour.

strategies.title: Scare tactics and fear appeals
strategies.description: Graphic images, stories of “victims” and exaggerated accounts of harms; may arouse curiosity, resistance or the belief that “it doesn't apply to me”.

strategies.title: Unstructured discussion groups about substances
strategies.description: Free-form talks about substance experiences in a group of high-risk young people; may reinforce norms favourable to use.

goodPractice.text: Use interactive methods (small-group work, role-play, discussion).
goodPractice.rationale: Interactive programmes show clearly better results than lecture-based ones because they allow skills to be practised.

standards.title: Quality standards and the system of recommended programmes in Poland
paragraphs: Poland has a System of Recommended Prevention and Mental Health Promotion Programmes. It was set up jointly by the institutions responsible for prevention: the former National Bureau for Drug Prevention (KBPN) and the State Agency for Prevention of Alcohol-Related Problems (PARPA) – merged in 2022 into the National Centre for Prevention of Addictions (KCPU) – together with the Centre for Education Development (ORE) and the Institute of Psychiatry and Neurology (IPiN).

Programmes submitted to the system are assessed by experts against shared quality criteria, including: being based on needs assessment and theory, clearly defined goals, appropriate methods, developed materials (manual, session plans), training of implementers and evaluation results. Depending on the strength of evidence, a programme may receive one of several recommendation levels (e.g. promising, good practice, model programme).

Recommended programmes are published in the online “Database of Recommended Programmes”. Schools and local authorities can choose programmes from it for the school's educational and prevention programme and for municipal programmes on prevention and solving addiction problems. Examples from the database include “Unplugged”, the “Strengthening Families Programme 10–14”, “School for Parents and Educators”, “Zippy's Friends” and “Fantastic Opportunities”.

When designing your own programme it is worth using the same criteria and the European Drug Prevention Quality Standards (EDPQS), which describe the whole project cycle: from needs assessment through planning and delivery to evaluation and dissemination.
Institution names, recommendation levels, the list of programmes and the current address of the database should be checked against the sources before use in coursework.

wizardHints.needs: Gather data about the setting: surveys, talks with pupils, teachers and parents, school or municipal data. Describe problems but also resources (people, places, readiness for change).
wizardHints.target: Define who the programme is for, their age and how many people it will reach. The prevention level follows from the group's level of risk, not from the topic.
wizardHints.factors: Choose a few risk factors to weaken and protective factors to strengthen – those confirmed by the assessment. Fewer, well-chosen ones work better.
wizardHints.goals: Write one general goal and several specific, measurable objectives (e.g. “participants can refuse under pressure – increase on a self-rating scale”).
wizardHints.strategies: Choose strategies with proven effectiveness and interactive methods. You can attach a session plan from the session builder to each strategy.
wizardHints.schedule: Plan the series of sessions over time (ideally several months with booster sessions), list implementers, venues, materials and budget.
wizardHints.evaluation: Assign an indicator and a measurement method to each objective. Measure before and after the programme; also collect feedback from participants and implementers.

indicatorExamples: percentage of participants stating an intention not to start drinking alcohol (pre/post)
change in pupils' estimates of the percentage of peers who use e-cigarettes
mean score on a refusal-skills scale (self-rating 1–5)
number of parents who completed at least 80% of sessions
sense of school bonding in a short survey (pre/post)
number of substance-related incidents reported at school during the school year
rating of sessions by participants and implementers (survey after each module)
